Millet
MIL-et
noun
“Millet” comes through Old French from Latin milium, a small-grained cereal grass (Panicum miliaceum). The name marks its many tiny seeds — from mille, a thousand.

Biblical Definition

In the KJV millet is a small grain, named but once, among the poor stuffs of Ezekiel’s siege-bread. The word is not archaic in sense — millet is still millet — but the modern reader, who thinks of it as birdseed or a health-food curiosity, must be told what it meant on that prophet’s table. When Ezekiel was made a sign of the coming siege of Jerusalem, the LORD commanded him: “Take thou also unto thee wheat, and barley, and beans, and lentiles, and millet, and fitches, and put them in one vessel, and make thee bread thereof” (Eze 4:9). No householder in plenty bakes bread of six grains and pulses swept together; that is famine-bread, the loaf of a city where the wheat is nearly gone and every last scraping must go into the pot. Millet, a coarse and humble grain, belonged to such a loaf. Behind the sign lies the sentence pronounced in Eden: “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Gen 3:19). Bread is never far from the curse and the toil of a fallen world, and in judgment it grows dear indeed: “We gat our bread with the peril of our lives because of the sword of the wilderness” (Lam 5:9). Yet even under judgment the ordinance of labour holds — “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10) — and the humble millet of the siege-loaf preaches that daily bread, coarse or fine, is the gift of God to be received with thanks and earned with toil.

Webster 1828 Definition

A small coarse cereal grain, named once, in the famine-bread of Ezekiel’s siege.

MILLET, a small-grained cereal grass (Panicum miliaceum); a humble bread-corn.

From Latin milium, akin to mille, a thousand — for its many tiny seeds.

Named once in Scripture, in the siege-bread of Ezekiel (Eze 4:9).

A coarse grain of the poor, fit for the loaf of a besieged and famished city.

It preaches that daily bread, however humble, is God’s gift and man’s labour.

Key Scripture

Eze 4:9 — "Take thou also unto thee wheat, and barley, and beans, and lentiles, and millet, and fitches, and put them in one vessel, and make thee bread thereof, according to the number of the days that thou shalt lie upon thy side, three hundred and ninety days shalt thou eat thereof."

Gen 3:19 — "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return."

Lam 5:9 — "We gat our bread with the peril of our lives because of the sword of the wilderness."

2Th 3:10 — "For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat."

Modern Corruption

No modern quarrel — only that we have forgotten millet was bread; and it preaches the doctrine of daily bread in a fallen and judged world.

expand to see more

Millet needs no rescue from a false modern sense; it needs only to be seen for what it was — food. To us it is fodder, or a fashionable grain in a bag from the health-shop; to the besieged of Jerusalem it was one of the last things left to bake. The whole force of Eze 4:9 hangs on the poverty of the mixture: wheat and barley are honest bread-corns, but beans, lentiles, millet, and fitches thrown into one vessel are the diet of desperation, weighed out by measure and eaten by measure, as the next verses show.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of daily bread. From Eden the sentence stood, “in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread”; and where men rebel, the LORD can make that bread scarce and dear, till a city bakes its millet by weight and eats it in fear. Let the well-fed Christian read Ezekiel’s loaf and repent of a careless heart. Every meal is mercy; the coarse grain no less than the fine is “our daily bread,” asked of the Father and earned by the sweat He appointed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A small coarse bread-grain, named once, in Ezekiel’s loaf of siege.

expand to see more

Millet — a small cereal grain, Latin milium.

Named for its many seeds — mille, a thousand.

A humble bread-corn of the poor (Panicum miliaceum).

Its one appearance is in the siege-bread of Ezekiel (Eze 4:9).

It preaches daily bread as gift and as toil in a fallen world.

Usage

"Millet in the KJV is bread-grain, not birdseed: the food of a famished city."

"Beans, lentiles, and millet in one pot — that is the loaf of a siege, not a feast."

"The coarse millet of Ezekiel’s loaf still preaches: give us this day our daily bread."
